0. FOREWORD

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 9 June 1959, after the draft finalized by the Methods of Chemical Analysis Sectional Committee had been approved bv the Structural and Metals `Division Council. 0.2 The methods of analysis prescribed in this standard have been prepared with a view that they shall be useful as reference methods. Due consideration has been given in the preparation of this standard to the facilities available in the country for such analysis. 0.3 Taking into consideration the views of the producers, consumers and testing authorities, the Sectional Committee responsible for the preparation of this standard felt that it should be related to the technological due methods followed in the country in this field. Furthermore, weightage had to be given to the need for international coordination among standards prevailing in different countries of the world. These considerations led the Sectional Committee to derive assistance from the 1956 Book of ASTM Methods for Chemical Analysis of Metals published by the American Society for Testing Materials. 0.4 This standard which is a necessary adjunct to IS : 24-1956 Specification for Brazing Solder ( Reviad ) requiies reference to the following Indian Standard Specifications: *IS : 264-1950 NITRICAcm *IS : 265-1950 HYDROCHLORIC ACID *IS : 266-1950 SULPHURIC ACID *IS : 1070-1957 DISTILLED WATER 0.4.1 Wherever a reference to any. specification mentioned under 0.4 appears in this standard, it shall be taken as a reference to the latest version of the specification. Od5 In view of the decision of the Government of India to introduce throughout the country a uniform system of weights and measures based on the metric system, all the values appearing in this standard have been expressed in the metric units only. ____
*Since revised.

2

IS:999-1959 0.6 In reporting the result of a test or analysis made& accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with *IS : 2-1949 Rules for Rounding off Numerical Values.

4. DETERMINATION OF COPPER AND LEAD OUSLY BY THE ELECTROLYTIC METHOD 4.1 Apparatus 491.1Platinum Electrodes -with

SIMULTANE-

or without rotating stirrer.

4.1.1.1 Cathode - It shall be formed either from a sheet or wire gauze and shall have a depositing surface of about 100 sq cm. 4.1.1.2 Anode - It shall be in the form of either spiral or made from wire gauze. The former is recommended when the anode serves also as a stirrer and the latter when samples contain above 0'2 percent of lead. 4.1.2 Beaker - It shall be 250- to 300-ml, tall-form lipless beaker with a well-fitting split cover glass. 4.2 Reagents 4.2.1 Dilute Nitric Acid -l:land1:99(byvolume). 4.2.2 Dilute Hydrochloric Acid - 0'1 N approximately. 4.2.3 Ethyl Alcohol ( Ethanol ) - 95 percent ( by volume ). 4.2.4 Methyl Alcohol ( Methanol ) - 95 percent ( by volume ). 4.3 Procedure 4.3.1 Dissolve two grams of the accurately weighed sample in 25 ml of dilute nitric acid ( 1 : 1 ). Heat on a steam-bath and boil gently to expel brown fumes. Add 50 ml of hot water and alldw to stand on a steam-bath for one hour. Add paper pulp and filter off the `metastannit acid through a close-texture filter paper into the 250-ml beaker. Wash several times with hot dilute nitric acid ( 1 : 99 ). 4.3.2 Add one drop of 0'1 N hydrochloric acid to the filtrate and dilute to 150 ml with water. Insert electrodes into the solution, cover the beaker with a pair of well-fitting split cover glass and electrolyse at a current density of 4 amperes per square decimetre using a gauze cathode. When the solution is colourless, wash down the split cover glass, electrodes and the sides of the beaker and continue the electrolysis at a lower current density of 0'3 amperes per square This will be indidecimetre, until the deposition of copper is complete. cated by the failure to plate on the new exposed surface of platinum when the level of the solution is raised. When no copper appears on the cathode, it can be assumed that all lead has also been deposited on the *Sincerevised. 5

IS : 999 - 1959 anode. Without breaking the current, raise the electrode assembly, rinse thoroughly with water and collect the washings into the electrolyte. Reserve the electrolyte for the determination of cadmium and zinc. Dip the cathode in successive baths of ethanol or methanol and dry in an air Dry the anode oven at 110�C for 3 to 5 minutes and weigh for copper. at 110 to 120�C for 30 minutes; the deposit being fragile should be Cool the anode and weigh as lead peroxide. handled with care. 4.4 Calculation Copper, percent Lead, percent where

5.3.1 Transfer the electrolyte reserved in accordance with 4.3.2 to a 600-ml beaker and boil to expel dissolved gases. Make the solution slightly alkaline with dilute ammonium hydroxide solution and then just neutral with dilute sdphuric acid ( 1 : 4 ). Add 25 ml of dilute sulphuric acid ( 1 : 4 ) `in excess, dilute to 300 ml with water, heat to boiling and pass hydrogen sulphide gas into the solution for one hour. Allow it to stand until the precipitate has settled and filter off impure 6

IS:999- 1959 cadmium sulphide in a loose-bottom Gooch crucible. Remove the precipitate by punching out the bottom of the Gooch crucible into a 200-ml beaker, wash and wipe the sides of the crucible with a little asbestos pulp. Add 60 ml of dilute sulphuric acid ( 1 : 5 ) and boil for 30 minutes. Filter, wash and add about 5 g of ammonium chloride to the filtrate. Dilute to 300 ml with water, heat to boiling and pass hydrogen sulphide gas into the solution for one hour. Allow it to stand until the precipitate has settled and filter. Reserve the combined filtrate for the determindtion of zinc. 33.2 Dissolve the precipitate of cadmium sulphide in 25 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid solution in a weighed platinum dish, add 10 ml of dilute sulphuric acid ( 1 : 1 ) and evaporate to dense white fumes. Remove the excess sulphuric acid by heating the dish cautiously, and finally heat to 500 to 600%. Cool and weigh as cadmium sulphate. 5.4 Calculation Cadmium, where A = weight in g of cadmium sulphate, and B = weight in g of the sample used. 6. 6.1.5 Test Lead - Lead containing not more O%Ol percent of copper and iron respectively.

6.1.6 Sodium Acetate-Acetic Acid Bu$M Solution -Dissolve 270 g of anhydrous sodium acetate in 500 ml of water, add 240 ml of acetic acid, cool and dilute to one litre. 6.1.7 Hydoxylamine Hydrochloride Solution ( NHEOH'HC~ ) - 10 g per litre. Dissolve one gram of the reagent in water and dilute to 100 ml.. 7

6.1.6 Ortho-phunthroline Solution -Two grams per litre. Dissolve O-2 g of ortho-phenanthroline monohydrate in 90 ml of water with stirring and gentle heat. Cool and dilute to 100 ml with water. 6.1.9 SturmkudIron Solution - ( 1 ml = 0.02 mg of Fe ). Dissolve : 0'140 5 g of ferrous ammonium sulphate [ Fe ( NH4 )s ( SOI )a ' 6HtO ] in - 100 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 19 ) and dilute to one litre in a volumetric flask. Prepare fresh.

6.2 Procedure 6.2.1 Transfer up to two grams of the accurately weighed sample, from which foreign iron particles have been removed, to a 250-ml wide mouth flask. Add 20 ml of hydrobromic acid-bromine mixture. If necessary, add a few drops of bromine to ensure complete dissolution and heat in a well-ventilated hood at low temperature to dryness. 6.2.2 Add 10 ml of perchloric acid and heat with continuous swirling over an open flame in a well-ventilated hood to expel bromides of tin and antimony. When copious white fumes of perchloric acid appear, heat gently and intermittently to decompose any lead bromide that may be present. After complete removal of stannic bromide, nitric acid may be added to destroy lead bromide, if persisting. If the solution is cloudy, showing incomplete removal of tin and antimony, add 5 ml of hydrobromic acid and repeat the fuming. Repeat hydrobromic acid treatment one or more times, if necessary, until fairly clear solution is obtained. Finally, add 15 ml of dilute sulphuric acid solution and evaporate to dense white fumes to expel perchloric acid. Continue heating until the volume of the solution has been reduced about two millilitres. Add 40 ml of water depending on the copper content of the sample under analysis, If there and one to two grams of test lead, and boil for 15 minutes. is any reason to suspect that the solution still contains more than two milligrams of copper, add one gram of test lead and boil for 10 minutes. Filter through a fine filter paper to remove lead, copper, etc. 6.2.3 Transfer the filtrate to a loo-ml volumetric flask. Dilute to 50 ml. Add 25 ml of sodium acetate-acetic acid buffer solution and shake well. Add two millilitres of hydroxylamine hydrochloride and 10 ml of o-phenanthroline solutions, dilute to the mark and shake well. 6.2.4 Transfer a suitable portion of the solution obtained in 6.2.3 to an absorption cell and take the photometric reading of the sobition using a light filter at 490 mp. 6.3 Cd&ration
Curve

I

6.3.1 Take a series of standard iron rolutions and a reagent blank. Using same quantities of reagents, carry through the entire stages of

IS:999-1959 procedure as described under 6.2 and record the photometric readings of all the standard solutions along with the blank one. Construct the calibration curve by plottinglthe photometric readings of standard solutions against the quantities of iron. 6.4 Calculation 6.4.1 Convert the photometricreading of the sample to milligrams of iron by means of the calibration curve, and calculate the percentage of iron as follows: Iron, percent = B X +J where

Just near the end point, dark blue solution turns suddenly yellowish green but changes back to blue. The end point is reached only when the yellowish green colour persists for 20 seconds. ISr999-1959 8.2.11 Standard Pdtassium Iodate Solution - 0.01 N approximately. Dissolve 0'356 7 g of the recrystallized potassium iodate in 200 ml of water containing one gram of sodium hydroxide and 10 g of potassium iodide. When the solution is complete, dilute to one litre with water. Standardize against tin or an alloy of tin, copper, zinc and lead using such an amount as to give approximately the same titration as the sample to be analysed. Reduce the tin and titrate with potassium iodate solution as described in 8.3. 8.2.12 Standard Iodine Solution - 0'01 N approximately. Dissolve 1'27 g of recrystallized iodine and 4 g of potassium iodide in 25 ml of water. When the solution is complete, dilute to one litre with water and store, cool place, in dark coloured glass-stoppered bottle. ganzardize the iodine s&tion as prescribed for potassiuni iodate solution under 8.2.11.
8.3 Procedure

8.3.1 Transfer 5 g of the accurately weighed sample to a 250-ml beaker, cover and dissolve in 5 ml of concentrated hydrochloric acid and 20 ml of dilute nitric acid solution adding more concentrated hydrochloric acid, if necessary, to keep the tin in solution. Heat on a steam-bath until the solution of the sample is complete and brown Add about 10 ml of ferric chloride solution, neutrafumes are expelled. lize with concentrated ammonium hydroxide and add a slight excess. Heat to boiling and filter through a rapid filter paper, and wash the beaker and precipitate several times with hot ammonium chloride solution. Dissolve the precipitate in hot dilute hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 1 ). Reprecipitate with coltcentrated ammonium hydroxide, boil, filter and wash thoroughly with -hot ammonium chloride solution. Remove the paper and the precipitate from the funnel and place it in a 500-ml conical flask. Add 25 ml of dilute hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 9 ) and swirl the flask to break up the paper. Dilute the solution to about 200 ml. Add 60 ml of concentrated hydrochloric acid, 2 drops of antimony chloride and 5 g of iron in the form of wire, strip or rod. Fit up the apparatus as shown in Fig. 2 and heat the solution to boiling with continuous evolution of gas for about 30 minutes. Some undissolved iron should remain after reduction. 8.3.2 After the reduction is complete, cool the contents of the flask to about 10% maintaining *an atmosphere of carbon dioxide by passing a current of the gas in the flask. Add 5 ml of starch solution and titrate with either standard potassium iodate or staddard iodine solution. 8.4 Calculation Tin, percent = AxB c x 100 12

I8.1.9 Standard Bismuth Solution- ( 1 ml = 0'000 1 g of Bi). Dissolve O'loOO g of pure bismuth metal in 10 ml of dilute nitric acid ( 1 : 1 ), add 2 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid and evaporate to fumes. Add 20 ml of water, heat to boiling and dilute to one litre. 10.2 Procedure 192.1 Transfer 10 to 50 g of the accurately weighed sample in a 400-ml beaker and add concentrated nitric acid at the rate of 40 ml per 10 g of the material. When the dissolution is complete, add 0'25 g of ferrous ammonium sulphate and boil for two minutes. Dilute to 200 ml with water and add concentrated ammonium hydroxide until the precipitated copper hydroxide is re-dissolved, and then add a little in excess. Add 10 ml of ammonium carbonate solution and heat to boiling. Allow the solution to stand overnight. Filter through a rapid filter paper and wash with hot ammonium hydroxide solution. Dissolve the precipitate through the filter paper with 20 ml of hot dilute sulphuric acid?.solution and wash with hot water. Re-precipitate with concentrated ammonium hydroxide, boil for two minutes and allow the precipitate to settle overnight. Filter and wash with hot dilute ammonium hydroxide solution to remove the copper completely and then twice with hot water. Dissolve the precipitate through the filter paper with 20 ml of hot dilute sulphuric acid solution, and wash thoroughly with hot water. Cool and add 10 ml of potassium iodide and 5 ml of sodium hypophosphite solutions. Allow the solution to stand for 10 minutes. If there is a precipitate, filter it off and wash with water. 10.2.2 Transfer the clear solution to one of a pair of matched IOO-ml Nessler tubes and dilute up to the IOO-ml mark. In the other tube put 20 ml of dilute sulphuric acid, 10 ml of potassium iodide and 5 ml of sodium hypophosphite solutions and dilute to a `few millilitres less than 100~ml mark. Into this tube, run the standard bismuth solution until the eolours in the two tubes match. Not more than 4 ml of the 17
